title: Nitzavim: you can return (Deuteronomy 30:1–3)
hookLine: however far scattered, a person and a people can return

lines: THE GAP IS NOT A WALL.
cards: You haven't called a friend in two years, so now it's too awkward to call. You stopped a practice, and starting again feels like admitting you ever stopped.
After a while, the distance itself becomes the reason you can't go back. The gap becomes the wall. Deuteronomy thirty is written for people standing on the far side of that gap.
And it says, again and again, that the gap is not a wall.

teach.b: The chapter imagines the worst. The blessings and the curses have all come true, and the people are scattered among the nations.
Then, it says, when you take it to heart there, wherever there is, and return to God and listen with all your heart and all your soul, God will return to you and gather you in.
Even, verse four adds, if you've been driven to the far edge of the heavens.
The Hebrew root running through these verses is shuv: turn, turn back, return. People return, God returns, the scattered are brought back.

From the same root comes teshuvah, usually translated repentance, but closer to returning. This portion is read in the season just before Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, the days most focused on teshuvah.
Notice what the text doesn't say. It doesn't say: if you never wander.
It assumes the wandering, and sets no distance beyond which return stops working. And notice the order: the people turn first, and then God turns too.

A step from one side is met by a step from the other. The medieval teacher Nachmanides reads the verses right after this, about a commandment that isn't too hard or too far away, as being about teshuvah itself.
Return, he says, is within reach.

how: Teshuvah, returning, is the central theme of the Hebrew month of Elul and the High Holy Days; Deuteronomy 30 is read in synagogue in the weeks just before Rosh Hashanah.

o: sitting, as students sit before a teacher
walking, as the people go into the land
standing, as the whole people stand together

games.q: inside the turning — tap the pairs.
p: not too far to be gathered

s: the chapter says return is only for those who never strayed far
even from the edge of the heavens.
teshuvah comes from a root meaning to turn back
in the chapter, only the people turn; God stays still
the people return, and God returns to them.

games.q: you've been away from something good for years, and it feels far too late. what does Deuteronomy 30 say?
o: past a certain distance, there's no way back.
return, even from the edge of the heavens, and be met.
wait until someone comes to find you.
games.why: the chapter assumes the wandering, sets no limit, and promises the step back will be met.

practice: Think of something good you've drifted from, a person, a habit, a place, a part of yourself, and notice any voice saying it's been too long.
Don't plan the whole road back; just find the first step, one message, one page, one short visit. Picture yourself taking it, and picture it being met.

wordCard.voice: Nitzavim. Standing. And in it, shuv: the turning back that the chapter says is always possible.

orig.note: Hebrew: return, repentance. from the root shuv, which runs through Deuteronomy 30:1–10.

carryVoice: Your line: you can return. No distance is too far for turning back. See you tomorrow.
